title: Episode 323: George II: Dettingen, the Jacobite Rising of '45, Culloden, and the Seven Years' War
description:
The dramatic, combative thirty-three-year reign of King George II. Pompous, punctual to a fault, yet possessing fearless physical courage, George II became the last British monarch in history to personally command an army in battle at Dettingen in 1743. In 1745, Bonnie Prince Charlie landed in Scotland, marching a Jacobite Highland army to Derby and throwing London into blind panic before the Duke of Cumberland crushed the rebellion at the bloody Battle of Culloden. Guided by his brilliant queen, Caroline of Ansbach, and wartime Prime Minister William Pitt the Elder, George's reign culminated in the 'Annus Mirabilis' of 1759, conquering Canada and India in the Seven Years' War. Discover Britain's warrior king.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the last British monarch to lead troops in battle with sword in hand: a king who defeated the Jacobites at Culloden and oversaw the birth of the British Empire: King George II. Here is George with the grand story of Dettingen and Bonnie Prince Charlie.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: QUEEN CAROLINE AND SIR ROBERT WALPOLE: 1727 TO 1737
When George II ascended the throne in June 1727 at age forty-three, he intended to immediately dismiss Sir Robert Walpole, whom he dismissed as a rogue. George was saved from political blunder by his remarkable wife, Queen Caroline of Ansbach. Caroline was an intellectual giant, a correspondent of Leibniz, and a woman of supreme diplomatic tact who recognized Walpole's indispensability. Working in secret alliance with Walpole, Caroline subtly guided her stubborn, vain husband, leading courtiers to recite the satirical court rhyme: 'You may strut, dapper George, but 'twill all be in vain; We know 'tis Queen Caroline, not you, that reign.' For a decade, Caroline and Walpole maintained peace, lowered taxes, and consolidated the Hanoverian regime. When Queen Caroline lay dying in November 1737 of a ruptured umbilical hernia, a poignant, famous scene occurred: as she urged her weeping husband to remarry after her death, George sobbed uncontrollably: 'Non, j'aurai des maîtresses!'—'No, I shall have mistresses!' Caroline gently replied: 'Ah, mon Dieu, cela n'empêche pas'—'My God, that does not prevent it.' Caroline's death broke George's heart, leaving him emotionally adrift. Queen Caroline's intellect was one of the finest of the eighteenth century: she debated philosophy with Samuel Clarke, corresponded with Gottfried Leibniz on theology, and introduced smallpox inoculation to Britain by testing the procedure on condemned Newgate prisoners before inoculating her own royal children. Her management of George II was a masterclass in psychological manipulation: she would sit with the King for hours listening to his boastful stories of his military prowess, gently planting ideas in his mind so that days later, the King would announce Walpole's policies as his own brilliant personal inventions. Her death in 1737 was a catastrophe for the monarchy, leaving George irritable, depressed, and increasingly stubborn.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BATTLE OF DETTINGEN: JUNE 27, 1743
George II's defining moment of personal glory arrived during the War of the Austrian Succession. In June 1743, George traveled to Germany to take personal command of the 'Pragmatic Army' of forty thousand British, Hanoverian, and Austrian troops. Trapped in a narrow valley near the Bavarian village of Dettingen between the River Main and steep wooded hills, surrounded by a superior French army under the Duke of Noailles, the Allied army faced annihilation. Fifty-nine-year-old King George II, wearing his yellow Hanoverian sash and his old crimson uniform from Oudenarde, rode forward to the front lines. When his frightened warhorse bolted toward the French lines, George reined in the beast, dismounted, drew his sword, and took his stand on foot among the British infantry, shouting in heavily accented English: 'Now boys, now for the honor of England! Fire, and behave valiantly, and the French will soon run!' Inspired by their king's courage, British infantry unleashed disciplined rolling musket volleys that shattered the French cavalry charges, winning a stunning victory. George II remains the last reigning British monarch ever to lead troops in person on the field of battle. At the Battle of Dettingen in June 1743, the fifty-nine-year-old monarch displayed the stubborn, fiery courage of his warrior ancestors. When the French cavalry charges threatened to overwhelm the British left, King George rode to the most exposed point of the line, his hat blown off by cannon shot. Refusing to seek safety, he rallied his soldiers on foot with sword drawn, standing shoulder-to-shoulder with private grenadiers under heavy artillery fire. George Frideric Handel celebrated the King's victory by composing the magnificent Dettingen Te Deum, a triumphant choral masterpiece performed at the Chapel Royal, sealing George II's enduring reputation as Britain's brave, soldier-monarch.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE 'FORTY-FIVE': BONNIE PRINCE CHARLIE LANDS IN SCOTLAND: 1745
In July 1745, the Stuart dynasty launched its final, most romantic, and most dangerous bid for the British crown: the Jacobite Rising of 'The Forty-Five'. Twenty-four-year-old Prince Charles Edward Stuart—universally known as 'Bonnie Prince Charlie'—landed on the remote Hebridean island of Eriskay with just seven companions. Raising the Stuart royal standard at Glenfinnan, the charismatic young prince rallied thousands of Highland clansmen. In September, the Jacobites marched into Edinburgh without resistance, proclaiming James VIII and III at the Mercat Cross. Days later, at the Battle of Prestonpans, the Highlanders unleashed their terrifying 'Highland Charge' through morning mist, routing Sir John Cope's government army in just ten minutes. In November, commanding five thousand men, Bonnie Prince Charlie crossed the border into England, capturing Carlisle, Lancaster, and Manchester, advancing as far south as Derby, just one hundred and twenty-seven miles from London. Bonnie Prince Charlie's landing in Scotland was an astounding romantic adventure that caught the British government completely off guard. Tall, athletic, with charming golden manners, the young prince adopted Highland dress, wearing tartan trews, eating oatmeal bannocks, and wading through rivers beside his men. At the Battle of Prestonpans, the Highland charge struck with terrifying savagery: firing a single musket volley at point-blank range, dropping their guns, and charging through the smoke with broadswords and dirks, the clansmen hacked through the Royal Army in minutes. Charles treated wounded government soldiers with chivalric mercy, establishing a court at Holyrood Palace that captivated Edinburgh society.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: BLACK FRIDAY AND THE TURNING POINT AT DERBY: DECEMBER 1745
On Friday, December 6, 1745, remembered in London history as 'Black Friday', terror seized the British capital: the Bank of England faced a catastrophic run on gold, shops shuttered, and King George II ordered his royal yachts prepared on the Thames to evacuate the royal family and treasury if necessary. Yet that very afternoon, at a tense war council inside Exeter House in Derby, the Jacobite leadership fractured. Lord George Murray and the clan chieftains argued that no English Jacobites had joined them, French invasion fleets had failed to materialize, and three government armies under the Duke of Cumberland were converging upon them. Bonnie Prince Charlie pleaded on his knees with tears in his eyes to march on London, convinced that the capital would collapse. His commanders overruled him, ordering an immediate retreat to Scotland. It was the fateful turning point of the rising: retreating northward in the winter snows, the Jacobites lost their momentum, their mystique, and their hope of victory. The panic in London on 'Black Friday', December 6, 1745, revealed the fragile psychological foundations of the Hanoverian regime. Diarist Horace Walpole recorded that Londoners expected the savage Highlanders to sack the city, with rumors claiming clansmen ate Protestant children. The decision to retreat from Derby, taken inside Exeter House, was bitterly opposed by Bonnie Prince Charlie, who threw himself onto his sofa weeping that he was betrayed. Historians still debate whether a continued march on London might have succeeded: while Cumberland's armies were in the field, London was lightly defended, and King George was prepared to fight in person on Finchley Common.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SLAUGHTER OF CULLODEN: APRIL 16, 1746
The apocalyptic climax came on April 16, 1746, on the bleak, windswept moor of Culloden near Inverness. Cornered, exhausted, and half-starved after a botched night march, five thousand Jacobites drew up their lines in driving sleet against nine thousand veteran government soldiers commanded by George II's younger son, twenty-five-year-old William Augustus, Duke of Cumberland. When the Highlanders launched their desperate charge across the sodden moor, Cumberland's troops unleashed devastating canister artillery and disciplined rolling musketry fire. Cumberland had drilled his infantry in a new bayonet tactic: instead of thrusting at the Highlander directly in front—whose targe shield blocked the blow—soldiers lunged diagonally at the exposed right side of the man to their right. Within forty minutes, the Jacobite army was annihilated: over fifteen hundred Highlanders were slaughtered, while Cumberland lost barely fifty men. Cumberland unleashed brutal reprisals across the Highlands, hunting down wounded men and burning crofts, earning the permanent moniker 'Sweet William' in England and 'The Butcher' in Scotland. Bonnie Prince Charlie escaped into the western isles with the aid of Flora MacDonald, fleeing to lifelong drunken exile in France. The Battle of Culloden in April 1746 was a slaughter that permanently extinguished the clan way of life in the Scottish Highlands. Cumberland's veteran troops, drilled in bayonet cross-thrusting, held their lines against the ferocious Highland charge, cutting down clan chieftains in heaps of corpses. Following the battle, Cumberland unleashed merciless pacification: cattle were stolen, villages torched, bagpipes and tartan banned under the Act of Proscription, and heritable jurisdictions abolished, ending feudal clan militarism forever. Bonnie Prince Charlie wandered as a hunted fugitive through the misty heather of Skye for five months before escaping to France, spending his remaining decades in bitter, drunken obscurity in Rome.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SEVEN YEARS' WAR AND THE 'ANNUS MIRABILIS': 1756 TO 1759
In the final decade of George II's reign, Great Britain fought the Seven Years' War—the first truly global war in human history, spanning North America, Europe, the Caribbean, and India. Initial British setbacks, including the loss of Minorca and General Braddock's slaughter in the Ohio wilderness, forced George II to appoint his bitter political critic, William Pitt the Elder, as wartime minister. Pitt possessed transcendent strategic vision: while funding Frederick the Great of Prussia to tie down French armies in Europe, Pitt deployed the Royal Navy to conquer France's overseas colonial empire. The year 1759 became Britain's 'Annus Mirabilis'—the Year of Miracles. In September 1759, General James Wolfe scaled the clifftops at night to defeat the French on the Plains of Abraham, capturing Quebec and winning Canada for the British Crown. In India, Robert Clive captured Bengal at Plassey. At Quiberon Bay, Admiral Edward Hawke smashed the French navy in a gale. Diarist Horace Walpole marveled: 'Our bells are worn threadbare with ringing for victories!' The Seven Years' War transformed Great Britain into a global colossus under the fiery wartime leadership of William Pitt the Elder. Pitt famously declared in the House of Commons: 'I know that I can save this country, and that no one else can!' Pitt coordinated global strategy with unmatched genius: subsidizing Prussian armies in Europe while dispatching British expeditions to the Caribbean, West Africa, and North America. The capture of Quebec on the Plains of Abraham in 1759 by thirty-two-year-old General James Wolfe—who died in the moment of victory hearing that the French were running—ended French rule in Canada forever, cementing British mastery of North America.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SUDDEN COLLAPSE AT KENSINGTON PALACE: OCTOBER 1760
By 1760, seventy-six-year-old King George II was blind in one eye, hard of hearing, yet proud of having lived to see his kingdom become the master of the oceans and the wealthiest empire on earth. On the morning of Saturday, October 25, 1760, George woke at six in the morning at Kensington Palace as usual, drank his cup of chocolate, and walked into his private water closet. Moments later, his German valet heard a loud crash. Rushing into the closet, the valet found the King slumped on the floor, bleeding from the head where he had struck a bureau in falling. Royal physicians were summoned, but seventy-six-year-old King George II was dead. A post-mortem autopsy revealed that he had suffered a rupture of the right ventricle of the heart—a thoracic aortic dissection. Buried beside Queen Caroline in Westminster Abbey, George had requested that the sides of their coffins be removed so their dust might mingle in eternity. George II passed the British crown to his twenty-two-year-old grandson, George III, the first Hanoverian monarch born and bred in England. George II's sudden death at Kensington Palace in October 1760 closed a pivotal thirty-three-year reign of dramatic expansion. Though often mocked for his thick German accent, explosive temper, and obsession with military uniforms, George II was a conscientious, brave monarch who never violated the British constitution or overrode parliamentary majorities. He left behind an empire stretching across five continents, an invincible Royal Navy, and an overflowing national wealth, passing the crown to his British-born grandson George III.

[Rebecca - Host]

Thank you for joining us for this episode of Most Fascinating Stories.
